items.label: text
items.text: Safety Note: Wear eye protection and avoid skin contact with the solution.

items.label: text
items.text: The experiment in Figure 20.21 is very simple and easy to set up. However, using this setup has the disadvantage that some oxygen will escape at the beginning of the reaction when MnO2 is added to H2O2 before the bung can be put back on the conical flask. Using a weighing bottle like the one in Figure 20.22 is a simple way of mixing the chemicals together without losing any oxygen before you can get the bung in. When you are ready to start the reaction, shake the flask so that the weighing bottle falls over and the manganese(IV) oxide comes into contact with the hydrogen peroxide. You need to keep shaking so that an even mixture is formed.

items.label: text
items.text: 'vol', meaning volume, is a measurement for concentration for hydrogen peroxide. 1 cm³ of 2 vol hydrogen peroxide solution decomposes completely to give 2cm³ of oxygen.

items.label: section_header
items.text: PRACTICAL: INVESTIGATE THE EFFECT OF DIFFERENT SOLIDS ON THE CATALYTIC DECOMPOSITION OF HYDROGEN PEROXIDE SOLUTION

items.label: text
items.text: Figure 20.21 shows apparatus that can be used to measure how the volume of oxygen produced changes with time.

items.label: text
items.text: The following procedure could be used:

items.label: list_item
items.text: Measure 100 cm³ of 2 vol hydrogen peroxide and transfer to a 250 cm³ conical flask.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Weigh out 0.20 g of manganese(IV) oxide on a balance.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Add the manganese(IV) oxide to the hydrogen peroxide and quickly replace the bung with the gas syringe already attached. Swirl the reaction mixture at a constant speed.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Record the amount of oxygen produced every 20 seconds for 3 minutes and plot a graph of volume of oxygen versus time.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Repeat the reaction with 0.20 g of lead(IV) oxide and copper(Il) oxide but keep everything else the same.

items.label: text
items.text: The sample data below show manganese(IV)oxide is a very effective catalyst for the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide. In comparison, lead(IV) oxide is less effective as the rate of the reaction is much slower and copper(ll) oxide does not act as a catalyst for this reaction at all.

items.text: Figure 20.23 The catalytic effect of different solids on the decomposition of H2O2.
